han-dynastie-und-seidenstrasse#text: Emperor Wu of Han sent the envoy Zhang Qian west to find allies against the mounted nomads of the Xiongnu. His reports on the lands of Central Asia led to regular caravans that carried silk, lacquer and iron westward and brought horses, glass, gold and later Buddhism to China. The Han dynasty ruled from 206 BC to AD 220, raised Confucianism to the state doctrine and established a civil service filled through examinations.
hopewell-kultur#title: The Hopewell culture and its exchange network
hopewell-kultur#summary: In the Ohio Valley, communities build geometric earthworks and exchange raw materials across half the continent.
hopewell-kultur#text: The Hopewell culture was centered in Ohio and Illinois. Its people laid out circles, squares and octagons of earthen walls, some of them aligned with the lunar standstills, and buried respected dead with rich grave goods in burial mounds. These graves contained copper from the Great Lakes, shells from the Gulf of Mexico, mica from the Appalachians and obsidian from the area of today's Yellowstone. Researchers call these far-reaching connections the Hopewell Interaction Sphere. The Newark Earthworks and other sites have been World Heritage since 2023.
sima-qian-schreibt-das-shiji#summary: The court historian Sima Qian completes the Records of the Grand Historian, the model for all later Chinese histories.
sima-qian-schreibt-das-shiji#text: Sima Qian continued his father's work and described in 130 chapters the history of China from the mythical Yellow Emperor to his own day under Emperor Wu of Han. He arranged the material into dynastic annals, tables, treatises and biographies, traveled to the places he wrote about and compared his sources critically. When he defended a disgraced general in 99 BC, he was sentenced to castration but chose to go on living in order to finish his work. For two thousand years the Shiji remained the model for the official dynastic histories.
spartacus-aufstand#summary: The gladiator Spartacus leads tens of thousands of escaped slaves against Roman armies for two years.
spartacus-aufstand#text: In 73 BC, Spartacus and about 70 gladiators broke out of a school in Capua and entrenched themselves on Mount Vesuvius. Slaves from the country estates and impoverished farm laborers joined them until the force grew to between 70,000 and 120,000 people and defeated several Roman armies. The march led as far as northern Italy and back south again, where pirates refused the promised passage to Sicily. In 71 BC Marcus Licinius Crassus defeated the rebels in Lucania; Spartacus fell in battle, and 6,000 prisoners were crucified along the Via Appia from Capua to Rome. The revolt was the largest slave war of antiquity and later became a symbol of the fight against oppression.
caesar-erobert-gallien#summary: Gaius Julius Caesar subdues all of Gaul up to the Rhine in eight years.
caesar-erobert-gallien#text: As governor, Caesar waged war against Celtic and Germanic tribes and in 52 BC defeated the uprising under Vercingetorix at Alesia. His accounts, the Gallic War, made him famous in Rome and turned his legions into a power base loyal to him alone. Gaul became a Roman province and was later Romanized.
ermordung-caesars#summary: On the Ides of March, Caesar is stabbed to death by senators around Brutus and Cassius.
ermordung-caesars#text: After his victory in the civil war against Pompey, Caesar had himself appointed dictator for life. A group of senators feared the end of the Republic and killed him on 15 March 44 BC. Instead of saving the Republic, the deed set off a new civil war at the end of which Octavian stood as sole ruler.
stele-2-von-chiapa-de-corzo#summary: A stela at Chiapa de Corzo bears the oldest known date of the Mesoamerican Long Count.
stele-2-von-chiapa-de-corzo#text: On a stone fragment from Chiapa de Corzo in southern Mexico, a date corresponding to December 36 BC is carved. It is the oldest known date of the Long Count, which counted days from a starting point in 3114 BC. The numbers are written with bars for five and dots for one. The system was probably not invented by the Maya but by peoples in the former Olmec region and in Chiapas; the Maya adopted and refined it and used it until the 10th century.
schlacht-bei-actium#summary: Octavian's fleet under Agrippa defeats Mark Antony and Cleopatra and ends the civil wars of the Republic.
schlacht-bei-actium#text: After Caesar's death, Octavian and Mark Antony had divided the empire between them, but Antony's association with Cleopatra and his grants of eastern territories to her children gave Octavian his pretext for war. On 2 September 31 BC the fleets met off the promontory of Actium on the west coast of Greece. Octavian's admiral Agrippa cut off Antony's heavy ships; Cleopatra and Antony escaped to Egypt with part of the fleet, and their troops surrendered. The following year Octavian took Alexandria, Antony and Cleopatra took their own lives, and Egypt became a Roman province. Actium ended almost a century of civil wars and made Octavian sole ruler.
tod-kleopatras#title: The Death of Cleopatra and the End of the Hellenistic Age
tod-kleopatras#summary: With the suicide of Cleopatra VII, the last Hellenistic kingdom falls to Rome.
tod-kleopatras#text: Cleopatra VII, the last ruler of the Ptolemaic line, had allied herself with Caesar and afterwards with Mark Antony in order to secure Egypt's independence. After the defeat in the naval battle of Actium in 31 BC and Octavian's entry into Alexandria, Antony and Cleopatra took their own lives. Egypt became a Roman province, and with that the age of the Hellenistic kingdoms that had grown out of Alexander's conquests came to an end.
augustus-begruendet-den-prinzipat#summar: Octavian receives the honorary name Augustus and becomes in effect the first Roman emperor.
augustus-begruendet-den-prinzipat#text: After his victory over Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC, Octavian claimed to be restoring the Republic while keeping control of the army, the provinces and the finances. As princeps, first among equals, he ruled for more than forty years and created the foundations of the imperial age. His reign brought internal peace and a cultural golden age with poets such as Virgil and Horace.
varusschlacht#title: The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
varusschlacht#summary: Germanic tribes under Arminius destroy three Roman legions.
varusschlacht#text: The Cheruscan chieftain Arminius, himself trained in Roman service, lured the governor Varus into an ambush. About 15,000 Romans lost their lives. Rome afterwards abandoned its plans to subdue the territory east of the Rhine for good; the Rhine and later the limes became the frontier.
buddhismus-erreicht-china#summary: Buddhist monks and scriptures reach China along the Silk Road, and the White Horse Temple is founded.
buddhismus-erreicht-china#text: According to tradition, Emperor Ming of Han dreamed of a golden figure and sent messengers west, who returned to Luoyang with two Indian monks and sutras carried on a white horse; there the first Buddhist temple in China was built. In fact, traders and monks from Central Asia brought the teaching into the country step by step, and translators such as An Shigao and later Kumarajiva rendered the scriptures into Chinese. In the troubled centuries after the end of the Han, the message of the end of suffering found a wide following; monasteries became landowners, places of learning and lenders.
ausbruch-des-vesuv#summary: The volcano buries Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and preserves them for posterity.
ausbruch-des-vesuv#text: Within a few hours the towns on the Bay of Naples were buried under ash, pumice and pyroclastic flows. Thousands of people died, among them the scholar Pliny the Elder. Excavations since the 18th century have given unique insight into everyday life in a Roman town.
eroeffnung-des-kolosseums#summary: Emperor Titus inaugurates the largest amphitheater of antiquity with a hundred days of games.
eroeffnung-des-kolosseums#text: From AD 72, Emperor Vespasian had an amphitheater built on the site of the artificial lake of Nero's palace, which his son Titus opened in AD 80 with a hundred days of gladiatorial combat, animal hunts and reportedly a mock naval battle; thousands of animals and many people died in the process. The structure of travertine, brick and concrete held about 50,000 spectators, who sat separated by rank and reached their seats within minutes through 80 numbered entrances; an awning provided shade, and lifts brought animals up from the cellars into the arena. It received the name Colosseum in the Middle Ages, after a colossal statue of Nero nearby. The games allowed the emperor to show himself to the people and prove his generosity; gladiatorial combat took place here until the 5th century.
kushan-reich-und-seidenstrasse#title: The Kushan Empire Links India to the Silk Road
kushan-reich-und-seidenstrasse#summary: Under King Kanishka the Kushans rule Central Asia and northern India and promote trade, Buddhism and the art of Gandhara.
kushan-reich-und-seidenstrasse#text: The Kushans, a people who had migrated from Central Asia, built an empire in the 1st century stretching from the Amu Darya to the Ganges, with capitals at Peshawar and Mathura. It lay at the crossroads of the trade routes between Rome, Persia, India and China and struck gold coins on the Roman model bearing Greek, Persian, Indian and Buddhist deities. Under Kanishka around 130, the first Buddha statues in human form were created in Gandhara, combining Greek and Indian stylistic elements. From here monks and texts of Mahayana Buddhism traveled to Central Asia and China.
moche-kultur#title: The Moche on the north coast of Peru
moche-kultur#summary: The Moche create irrigated oases, adobe pyramids and masterly pottery and goldwork.
moche-kultur#text: In the river valleys of Peru's north coast, the Moche channeled water from the Andes onto their fields through canals. Their rulers had huge pyramids of adobe bricks built, such as the Huacas del Sol y de la Luna near Trujillo. Moche potters shaped lifelike portrait vessels and painted pottery with scenes of war, ritual and everyday life. In 1987 Walter Alva found the untouched tomb of a ruler with gold and silver jewelry at Sipán, and in 2005 the Lady of Cao, a high-ranking woman, was discovered at El Brujo. Severe El Niño storms probably contributed to the decline of the Moche.
teotihuacan-metropole#summary: In the Valley of Mexico a planned city grows into the largest in the Americas.
teotihuacan-metropole#text: Teotihuacan was laid out along a grand avenue several kilometers long, which the Aztecs later called the Avenue of the Dead. Along it rise the Pyramid of the Sun, the Pyramid of the Moon and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent. Around AD 500 perhaps 100,000 people lived here in large apartment compounds, including migrants from Oaxaca and the Maya region. The city controlled the mining of obsidian and influenced art and politics as far as Guatemala. Around 550 the center burned down and the city lost its power; to the Aztecs it later counted as the place where the gods came into being.
erfindung-des-papiers#title: The Invention of Paper in China
erfindung-des-papiers#summary: The court official Cai Lun presents the emperor with an improved method of making paper.
erfindung-des-papiers#text: In the year 105, Cai Lun described a process in which tree bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets were pounded into a pulp, scooped onto screens and dried. Older paper finds show that simple papers already existed, but now the cheap material replaced bamboo slips and silk. The knowledge reached Japan by way of Korea and, after 751, passed through Arab workshops in Samarkand and Baghdad to reach Europe in the 12th century.
groesste-ausdehnung-unter-trajan#title: The Empire at Its Greatest Extent under Trajan
groesste-ausdehnung-unter-trajan#summary: With the conquest of Dacia, Armenia and Mesopotamia, the Roman Empire reaches its greatest extent under Trajan.
groesste-ausdehnung-unter-trajan#text: Trajan, the first emperor from a province, subdued the Dacian kingdom north of the Danube in two wars from 101 to 106, and its gold mines filled the treasury; Trajan's Column in Rome tells the campaign in a relief band 200 meters long. In 106 the Nabataean kingdom with Petra became the province of Arabia. From 114 Trajan marched against the Parthians, conquered Armenia and Mesopotamia and reached the Persian Gulf, where he is said to have regretted being too old for a campaign to India. At his death in 117 the empire covered about five million square kilometers and more than 60 million people. His successor Hadrian immediately gave up the eastern conquests because they could not be held.
bau-des-hadrianswalls#summary: Emperor Hadrian has a wall 118 kilometers long built across northern Britain as the frontier of the empire.
bau-des-hadrianswalls#text: Hadrian broke with the expansionist policy of his predecessor Trajan and secured the frontiers instead. During his visit to Britain in 122 he ordered the construction of a stone wall from the North Sea to the Irish Sea, up to four and a half meters high, with ditches, forts every Roman mile, watchtowers and garrisons in which about 10,000 soldiers from all parts of the empire served. The wall was meant less to repel attacks than to control movement, trade and customs. Wooden tablets from the fort of Vindolanda, with letters, shopping lists and a birthday invitation, give a unique glimpse of everyday life on the frontier. Rome also built fortified frontier lines along the Rhine and the Danube with the limes.
constitutio-antoniniana#title: Constitutio Antoniniana: Citizenship for All Free Inhabitants
constitutio-antoniniana#summary: Emperor Caracalla grants Roman citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire.
constitutio-antoniniana#text: Until 212, only Italians, veterans, elites of the provincial cities and freedmen were Roman citizens, while the majority of provincial inhabitants lived as peregrines under their own law. With an edict partly preserved on a papyrus in Giessen, Caracalla made all free inhabitants of the empire citizens. He gave thanks to the gods as his motive; the historian Cassius Dio suspected that the emperor wanted to extend the inheritance and manumission taxes, paid only by citizens, to everyone. The consequences were far-reaching: Roman law now applied to everyone from Britain to Syria, millions of people took the name Aurelius, and the distinction between conquerors and conquered disappeared.
sassanidenreich#title: Ardashir I Founds the Sasanian Empire
sassanidenreich#summary: A Persian prince overthrows the Parthians and builds an empire that is Rome's and Byzantium's great rival for four centuries.
sassanidenreich#text: Ardashir I of the Sasanian family defeated the last Parthian king in 224 and had himself crowned King of Kings; his capital became Ctesiphon on the Tigris. The Sasanians deliberately linked themselves to the Achaemenids, made Zoroastrianism the state religion and created a tight administration with noble ranks and standing armies of armored cavalry. Shapur I took the Roman emperor Valerian prisoner in 260, and in the 6th century Khosrow I reformed taxation and the army and supported the academy of Gundeshapur. Decades of war with Byzantium exhausted the empire, so that it fell to the Arab conquerors between 636 and 651.
reichskrise-des-3-jahrhunderts#title: The Crisis of the Third Century
reichskrise-des-3-jahrhunderts#summary: For fifty years, soldier emperors, civil wars, plagues, inflation and invasions by Germanic peoples and Persians shake the empire.
reichskrise-des-3-jahrhunderts#text: With the murder of Severus Alexander in 235 began a period in which the legions proclaimed and overthrew more than twenty emperors, hardly one of whom died a natural death. Goths plundered Greece and Asia Minor, Alemanni and Franks pushed into Gaul and Italy, and the Persian king Shapur I captured Emperor Valerian in 260. Gaul and Palmyra under Queen Zenobia broke away for a time as separate empires. The emperors debased the silver coinage until the denarius was almost pure copper, prices multiplied, and cities shrank behind new walls. Aurelian reunited the empire between 270 and 275; only Diocletian ended the crisis in 284 with sweeping reforms.
aksum-praegt-eigene-muenzen#summary: The kingdom of Aksum in the Ethiopian highlands becomes one of the few powers of its time to strike gold, silver and bronze coins.
aksum-praegt-eigene-muenzen#text: Aksum lay in the highlands of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea and, through the port of Adulis, controlled trade between the Roman Empire, Arabia and India. Under King Endubis, around 270, it began minting its own coins with Greek inscriptions, which were used in the long-distance trade of the Red Sea. Exports included ivory, gold, incense and animals from the interior. In the 3rd century the Persian religious founder Mani counted Aksum, alongside Rome, Persia and China, among the four great empires of the world. Huge stone stelae in the capital still bear witness to the power of its kings.
stele-29-von-tikal#title: Stela 29 at Tikal: the start of the Classic Maya period
stele-29-von-tikal#summary: The oldest dated stela of the Maya lowlands marks the beginning of the Classic period.
stele-29-von-tikal#text: Stela 29 from Tikal bears a Long Count date corresponding to the year AD 292. It shows a richly dressed ruler and is the oldest securely dated monument of its kind in the Maya lowlands. Researchers use it to mark the start of the Classic period, in which kings recorded their accessions, wars and rituals on stone monuments. Over the following six centuries, dozens of rival kingdoms with splendid capitals arose. Tikal itself, with its tall temple pyramids, became one of the most powerful cities.
tetrarchie-diokletians#summary: Diocletian divides rule over the empire among four emperors and reforms administration, army and taxation.
tetrarchie-diokletians#text: Diocletian, an officer from Dalmatia, recognized that a single emperor could no longer defend the threatened frontiers everywhere. In 286 he made Maximian co-emperor for the West, and in 293 each of them received a junior emperor, Constantius and Galerius, who were to succeed them. This rule of four governed from residences near the frontiers such as Trier, Milan, Sirmium and Nicomedia. Diocletian doubled the number of provinces, separated civil and military offices, introduced a new tax system and in 301 an edict on maximum prices, and in 303 launched the last great persecution of Christians. In 305 he became the only emperor to abdicate voluntarily and withdrew to his palace in Split; the tetrarchy soon broke apart in civil wars, from which Constantine emerged.
mailaender-vereinbarung#title: The Edict of Milan: Freedom of Religion for Christians
mailaender-vereinbarung#summary: Constantine and Licinius grant the long-persecuted Christians the free practice of their religion.
mailaender-vereinbarung#text: After centuries of intermittent persecution, Christians received full freedom of religion in 313 and the return of their confiscated property. Constantine supported the church, convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 and was baptized on his deathbed. In 380 Emperor Theodosius declared Christianity the state religion.
gupta-reich#title: The Gupta Empire as India's Golden Age
gupta-reich#summary: Under the Gupta kings, scholarship, literature and art in northern India enjoy a golden age.
gupta-reich#text: Chandragupta I founded a dynasty around 320 that under Samudragupta and Chandragupta II ruled most of northern India. The poet Kalidasa worked at the court, the astronomer Aryabhata calculated the circumference of the Earth and the value of pi, and Indian mathematicians developed the place-value system with the digit zero. The cave temples of Ajanta with their wall paintings and classical Sanskrit literature date from this period. In the middle of the 6th century the empire fell apart under the attacks of the Hunas from Central Asia.
konzil-von-nicaea#summary: At Constantine's invitation, about 300 bishops fix the Christian creed and condemn the teaching of Arius.
konzil-von-nicaea#text: The dispute between the Alexandrian priest Arius, who regarded Christ as a creature of God and subordinate to him, and his bishop split the church in the East. Constantine, who wanted unity of empire and church, summoned all bishops in 325 to his residence at Nicaea in Asia Minor and took part in the sessions himself. The council declared Christ to be of one substance with the Father, formulated the Nicene Creed that is still spoken in services today, and settled the date of Easter and the ranking of bishops. The Arians were banished, but the dispute went on for decades, and many Germanic peoples adopted Christianity in its Arian form. Nicaea was the first ecumenical council and established the close bond between emperorship and church.
ezana-christianisierung-aksum#summary: Ezana of Aksum converts to Christianity and makes his kingdom one of the first Christian states in the world.
ezana-christianisierung-aksum#text: Frumentius, a Christian from Tyre, had come to the court of Aksum as a young man and became tutor to the heir to the throne, Ezana. After being consecrated bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria, he worked to spread Christianity in the kingdom. Ezana adopted the new faith around 330; on his coins the cross replaced the older symbols of sun and moon. His inscriptions in Ge'ez, Greek and Sabaean also report campaigns as far as Meroe on the Nile. For centuries the Ethiopian church remained closely tied to the church of Alexandria.
teotihuacan-eingriff-in-tikal#summary: A general from Teotihuacan arrives at Tikal, the king dies on the same day, and a new dynasty takes power.
teotihuacan-eingriff-in-tikal#text: Maya inscriptions report that in January 378 a man named Siyaj K'ahk' arrived at Tikal. On the same day King Chak Tok Ich'aak died, probably by violence. Soon afterward Yax Nuun Ahiin ascended the throne, the son of a ruler closely tied to Teotihuacan. Thereafter warriors with weapons and clothing in the style of Teotihuacan appear at Tikal and other Maya cities. The event shows how closely the great centers of Mesoamerica were intertwined across hundreds of kilometers.
reichsteilung-395#title: The Division of the Roman Empire
reichsteilung-395#summary: After the death of Theodosius, the empire is finally divided into East and West.
reichsteilung-395#text: Theodosius left the West to his son Honorius and the East to his son Arcadius. The Greek-speaking East with Constantinople remained economically strong, while the West fell apart under pressure from Goths, Vandals and Huns. In 410 the Visigoths under Alaric sacked Rome.
marajoara-kultur#title: The Marajoara culture at the mouth of the Amazon
marajoara-kultur#summary: On the island of Marajó, settlements on artificial mounds and a rich art of pottery emerge.
marajoara-kultur#text: On the large river island of Marajó at the mouth of the Amazon, people built up earthen mounds from about AD 400 that stayed dry during floods and carried villages, graves and ceremonial sites. The painted burial urns with human faces and geometric patterns are famous. The Marajoara culture is part of the evidence that Amazonia was by no means untouched wilderness. Recent research with laser scans has also revealed causeways, canals and town-like settlements in Bolivia and Ecuador, and the dark earth created by humans, terra preta, is still fertile today.
pluenderung-roms-410#title: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths
pluenderung-roms-410#summary: The Visigoths under Alaric take Rome and plunder for three days a city no enemy had entered for 800 years.
pluenderung-roms-410#text: The Visigoths had fled across the Danube into the empire in 376 to escape the Huns and had destroyed a Roman army at Adrianople in 378. Their king Alaric demanded land and offices for his people; when the western court at Ravenna stalled him and had his negotiating partner Stilicho executed, he besieged Rome three times. On 24 August 410 traitors opened the Salarian Gate, and the Goths plundered palaces and temples for three days, though they spared the churches. The news shook the world; Jerome wrote that the city which had conquered the whole world had itself been conquered, and Augustine wrote The City of God in response. Alaric died the same year; the Visigoths later founded a kingdom in southern Gaul and Spain.
attila-und-die-hunnen#summary: On the Catalaunian Plains, Romans and Visigoths halt the Hunnic king Attila; his empire falls apart after his death in 453.
attila-und-die-hunnen#text: The Huns, a horse people from the steppes of Asia, had been driving the Goths before them since 375 and thereby set off the Migration Period. Attila, their king from 434, ruled from Hungary an empire stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea, extorted annual payments of gold from the Eastern Empire and invaded Gaul in 451 with an enormous army. The Roman commander Aetius allied himself with the Visigothic king Theodoric I, who fell in the battle on the Catalaunian Plains near Troyes; Attila had to withdraw. In 452 he laid waste to northern Italy but turned back after a meeting with Pope Leo I. After his sudden death in 453, the Hunnic empire collapsed within a few years, but the Western Empire was so weakened that it lasted only two more decades.
ende-westroms#title: The End of the Western Roman Empire
ende-westroms#summary: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman emperor.
ende-westroms#text: The Germanic commander Odoacer sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople and ruled Italy as king. The event is traditionally regarded as the end of antiquity and the beginning of the Middle Ages, even though Roman administration, language and church survived for a long time in the Germanic successor kingdoms.
taufe-chlodwigs#title: The Baptism of Clovis and the Rise of the Frankish Kingdom
taufe-chlodwigs#summary: The Frankish king Clovis is baptized a Catholic at Reims and lays the foundation of the leading power in Western Europe.
taufe-chlodwigs#text: Clovis of the Merovingian line had defeated the last Roman governor in Gaul in 486 and united the Frankish subtribes. Around 498 he was baptized by Bishop Remigius at Reims, reportedly after a vow made in battle against the Alemanni. Because, unlike most Germanic kings, he chose the Catholic rather than the Arian confession, he won the support of the church and of the Roman population. After his victory over the Visigoths in 507 he ruled almost all of Gaul; his kingdom became the nucleus of France and Germany.
tiwanaku-am-titicacasee#summary: At an altitude of almost 4,000 meters, Tiwanaku becomes the religious and political center of the southern Andes.
tiwanaku-am-titicacasee#text: Tiwanaku lay near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca in today's Bolivia. The city had temple platforms such as the Akapana, sunken courts and the famous Gateway of the Sun, which shows a deity holding two staffs. Around the city farmers laid out raised fields whose water channels protected the plants from night frost and allowed high yields. Llama caravans linked Tiwanaku with colonies on the Pacific coast and in the lowlands. A long drought probably contributed to the city's decline after 1000; for the Inca, Lake Titicaca remained a sacred place of origin.
kaleb-feldzug-nach-himyar#summary: King Kaleb of Aksum crosses the Red Sea and conquers the kingdom of Himyar in present-day Yemen.
kaleb-feldzug-nach-himyar#text: In the southern Arabian kingdom of Himyar, the Jewish king Yusuf As'ar, called Dhu Nuwas in Arabic sources, had the Christians of the city of Najran persecuted around 523. Kaleb of Aksum, who saw himself as protector of the Christians, then landed in Arabia with an army and defeated him. For several decades southern Arabia stood under Aksumite influence, later under the Aksumite commander Abraha, who made himself independent. The campaign shows how closely Aksum was bound up with the world beyond the Red Sea. Around 570 the region was lost to the Persian Sasanian Empire.
benedikt-gruendet-montecassino#title: Benedict of Nursia Founds Monte Cassino
benedikt-gruendet-montecassino#summary: With the monastery of Monte Cassino and his Rule, Benedict founds Western monasticism.
